transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess... it's actually a bit of a long story, but I'll try to explain it properly. I'm a composer and a music director, and, well, for almost two years now—pretty much exactly since this one particular commission wrapped up, which was supposed to be this really significant milestone for me after finishing my graduate degree, you know? But ever since that commission, I’ve just been completely unable to shake this... this absolute certainty that a few specific people in the ensemble have been actively, but very quietly, undermining my work. 

And it’s not like they’re standing up and shouting during a performance, it’s... it’s insidious. It’s the schedule changes, for one. Suddenly a sectional rehearsal gets moved at the last minute. Or... or it's the seating choices. I’ll walk in and the acoustic balance is completely thrown off because someone decided to swap chairs, which they know perfectly well ruins the blend of the strings for my pieces. And then there are these little comments, just these tiny, almost imperceptible remarks during rehearsals that are clearly designed to chip away at my authority on the podium. 

And the most frustrating part—and I guess why I finally agreed to come in and talk to someone—is that whenever I try to address it, they always have this perfectly manufactured paper trail. They’ll pull up emails or, you know, administrative notes that supposedly explain the chair swaps or the time changes, like, "Oh, the hall was double-booked," or whatever excuse they've decided on. But... I mean, you can only see so many of these supposed explanations before you realize what's actually happening right in front of you. It's been almost two years of this constant maneuvering, and it's just... it takes a toll.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I have a very trained ear, obviously, given my profession. When you spend hours every day analyzing the minutiae of pitch and timbre, you become incredibly attuned to sound. I hear the subtle shifts in intonation from the second violins, or the way the oboe might be just a hair flat on a humid day. So if there were actual voices—like auditory hallucinations or something, which I assume is what you're getting at—I would absolutely be the first to notice. But no, the things I'm talking about, the remarks from the ensemble members, those are very real, very physical sounds coming from actual people in the room. It’s the whispering during rests, the muttered comments when I turn my back to check the score... it’s all real people, using real words, just carefully calculated to disrupt the rehearsal. But disembodied voices? No, never. My hearing is perfectly grounded in reality, which is exactly why I can tell when they're whispering about me.
Have you ever felt that someone could put thoughts into your mind or take thoughts out of it?

Put thoughts into my mind? Or take them out? No, no, definitely not. I mean, honestly, as a composer, my mind is essentially my... my sanctuary, really. It's my primary instrument. Everything I do starts there. When I'm conceptualizing a new piece—whether it's a full orchestral movement or just a really intimate chamber arrangement—the thematic material, the counterpoint, the harmonic progressions... all of that has to be generated entirely from within. 

It requires an immense amount of focus to hold a complex, multi-layered musical texture in your head before you even write a single note down on staff paper. If someone were somehow tampering with my thoughts, or... or extracting them, I wouldn't be able to function creatively at all. I wouldn't be able to hold those structures together. So, no, my thoughts are completely my own, very organized, and very deliberate. 

And honestly, I think that's exactly why this whole situation with the ensemble is so incredibly frustrating to me. Because my internal vision for the music is perfectly clear and entirely mine, but then I step onto the podium and have to deal with these external, physical disruptions they keep engineering. They aren't messing with my head or my thoughts, they're messing with the real, tangible elements of the rehearsal. My mind is perfectly intact and entirely my own territory.
Apart from these people in the ensemble undermining you, have you had any other strong beliefs that others would say are untrue or hard to believe?

No, no, I don't think so. I mean, I really try to pride myself on being a very rational, very grounded person. You sort of have to be when you're managing a large group of musicians, right? You have to deal with logistics, with budgets, with union rules about break times... it’s all very practical, very concrete stuff. I don't have time for, you know, flights of fancy or bizarre conspiracy theories about the government or aliens or whatever it is people come up with. 

My whole life is just music and the reality of getting that music performed. I don't have any other... what did you call it? Strong beliefs? Everything else in my life is completely normal, completely mundane, really. I wake up, I write, I analyze scores, I deal with administration, and I try to get through rehearsals without someone intentionally sabotaging the cello section's bowing. 

So, no, there’s nothing else. It’s just this one very specific, very real, very documented—well, documented in the sense that I see it happening, even if their paperwork says otherwise—issue with this particular group of people. If it weren't for them, my professional life would be exactly what I envisioned it would be when I finished my master's degree. I just want to do my job, you know? I just want the music to sound the way it's supposed to sound. So, no, no other strange beliefs. Just the reality of what I'm dealing with on the podium.
If someone showed you clear proof that these ensemble members were not undermining you, would you be able to accept that?

Clear proof? I mean... well, see, that’s the thing. What even constitutes clear proof in a situation like this? Because, honestly, they already try to do exactly that. They *do* show me things. 

I’m actually here, sitting in this office, because for almost two years now I’ve been completely unable to shake the certainty of what's happening, and their so-called proof doesn't change it. It all started right after the commission. That commission was supposed to be a massive stepping stone for me, a really high-profile premiere, and almost immediately after it was announced, a few specific people in the ensemble just... shifted. They started using these highly coordinated, administrative tactics to quietly undermine my work. 

I'm talking about sudden schedule changes that completely derail my rehearsal plans and exhaust the brass section before we even get to the heavy movements. I'm talking about bizarre seating choices that deliberately mess with the acoustic balance of the strings. And, like I said before, those little comments in rehearsals that are timed perfectly to break my concentration when I'm on the podium. 

And when I call them out on it, or when I try to get the administration to step in, they always have some piece of paper ready. They show me emails from the venue, or personnel notes that supposedly explain why the schedule had to change, or why the principal violist had to be moved. On paper, it looks perfectly innocent, right? It looks like standard orchestral bureaucracy. But you have to understand, that's exactly how you quietly sabotage a director without getting caught. You hide it behind red tape. 

So, if someone showed me more of these emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away... no, I wouldn't just accept it. Because I've been living this for two years. I know the difference between a genuine logistical issue and a calculated attempt to ruin my music, no matter what their forwarded emails claim. I know what I'm experiencing.
Before this started with the ensemble, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?

No, not at all. Actually, quite the opposite, really. I mean, before all of this started with the commission and the ensemble, I was... well, I was incredibly trusting. Maybe even a bit naive, looking back on it now. 

When you're in a conservatory environment, especially in the composition and conducting programs, there's this profound sense of camaraderie. You're all in the trenches together, you know? You're staying up until three in the morning analyzing Mahler scores, or you're sight-reading each other's terrible first drafts in practice rooms that smell like old rosin and stale coffee. You have to trust your colleagues implicitly because you're literally placing your art—your most vulnerable, raw creations—into their hands. 

I always assumed everyone was operating in good faith. If a player told me a passage was unplayable, I believed them and I rewrote it. If a professor gave me harsh feedback, I took it as a genuine attempt to make me a better musician. I never, ever thought people had ulterior motives. I just assumed we all shared the same primary goal, which was to serve the music. To make the best possible art. 

Even when I first started working with this specific ensemble, before the commission was announced, I was completely open. I was inviting them out for drinks after rehearsals, asking for their input on bowing techniques... I wanted it to be this deeply collaborative, trusting environment. 

So, no, I didn't walk into this situation looking for shadows. I didn't have this pre-existing paranoia or distrust of people. I was just a composer trying to build relationships with the musicians who were going to bring my work to life. The distrust only came later, when it became absolutely, undeniably clear that my trust was being weaponized against me by these specific individuals. It wasn't how I was before, it's just what I've been forced to become to protect my work.
Have there been times when your thoughts felt jumbled or it was hard to keep them organized when you were speaking?

Jumbled? No, I don't... I don't think so. I mean, my thoughts are actually incredibly organized, maybe almost to a fault. You know, when you're writing a full orchestral score, you're essentially holding an entire sonic architecture in your head all at once. You have to know exactly what the flutes are doing in measure forty-seven while simultaneously understanding how that relates to the harmonic progression in the low brass and the rhythmic ostinato in the percussion. It requires an intense level of focus and mental clarity. If my thoughts were jumbled, I wouldn't be able to compose a single measure, let alone manage a sixty-piece ensemble.

And when I'm speaking, especially when I'm on the podium, I have to be completely precise. If I'm trying to explain a complex metric modulation to the strings, I can't afford to be disorganized or vague. I have to communicate exactly what I want, clearly and efficiently, because rehearsal time is incredibly expensive. We're talking hundreds of dollars a minute, sometimes. So, no, my thoughts are very clear. They have to be. 

Even when I'm trying to explain all of this... this situation with the ensemble undermining me... I feel like I'm laying it out very logically. I'm connecting the dots for you, showing you the sequence of events—the commission, the sudden schedule changes, the acoustic sabotage. It's all very linear, very rational. I don't feel like I'm jumping around or losing my train of thought. I'm just trying to give you the full picture, because the details matter. The details are where they hide their sabotage. So, no, I wouldn't say my thoughts are jumbled at all. If anything, they're hyper-focused on the reality of what's happening to my music.
Have you had a period where you felt unusually high, energetic, or irritable for days at a time?

High? Energetic? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, look, conducting takes energy, obviously. When you're up there on the podium for a three-hour rehearsal of a Mahler symphony, you are physically exerting yourself. You're sweating, your heart rate is up, you're projecting your voice over an entire orchestra. It's an intensely physical job. And yes, there's a certain adrenaline rush that comes with a performance, a kind of... elevated state where you're completely connected to the music and the musicians. But that's just the nature of the work, you know? It's not an unusual high, it's just the baseline requirement for being a conductor. 

And as for being irritable... well, I've certainly been frustrated. Incredibly frustrated. But I think anyone in my position would be. When you have dedicated your entire life to a piece of music, when you've agonized over every single articulation mark and dynamic shift, and then you see people actively, deliberately trying to dismantle it... yes, that makes me angry. It makes me irritable when they switch the rehearsal schedule at the last minute and I have to scramble to restructure the entire session. It makes me irritable when the principal oboist suddenly decides to take a tempo marking completely out of context and ruins the phrasing of an entire section, and then looks at me like it was just an innocent mistake. 

But it's not some... unexplained, days-long mood swing. It's a direct, proportional reaction to the sabotage I'm dealing with. If they would just stop trying to ruin my work, if they would just play the notes as written and respect the rehearsal process, I wouldn't be irritable at all. I would just be focused on the music. So, no, I haven't had any periods of being unusually high or energetic, and my irritability is completely tied to the very real things these people are doing to undermine my career.
Do you believe with complete certainty that these ensemble members are deliberately undermining you?

Yes. Yes, absolutely. I mean, that's... that's exactly why I'm here, really. For almost two years now, I have been completely, undeniably certain that this is happening. Ever since that commission was announced, it’s been this ongoing, systematic campaign to quietly dismantle my work. 

And I know how it sounds, I really do, but when you look at the sheer volume of it... the schedule changes that always seem to happen right before a critical run-through, or the seating choices—like moving the horns just far enough back that the acoustic balance is completely thrown off in the hall we use. And the little comments during rehearsals. Oh, the comments. They’ll say things like, "Are you sure about this tempo marking?" or "This phrasing feels a bit unnatural, don't you think?" in front of the entire ensemble, just planting these little seeds of doubt about my competence. 

And the thing is, they always have an excuse. They'll show me an email chain supposedly proving that the venue double-booked us, or they'll bring in some acoustic study about horn placement, or they'll point to a note in the score that they claim is ambiguous. They always have this perfectly crafted, plausible deniability ready to go. But you can't have that many "coincidences" over a two-year period. You just can't. It's deliberate. It's calculated. And no matter what pieces of paper they wave in my face to supposedly explain it all away, I know exactly what they're doing. I can't shake it, because it's the truth.
Since this began, have you become less able to do your work or manage day-to-day life?

Less able? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I am still working just as much as I ever was. I haven't lost any commissions, I haven't stepped down from any podiums, and I certainly haven't stopped taking care of myself. My day-to-day life—eating, keeping my apartment in order, maintaining my physical stamina—all of that is perfectly fine. I know I have to stay sharp to deal with this. But... I will admit that the process of actually doing the work, the day-to-day logistics of it, takes so much more energy now. A tremendous amount of energy, actually. 

Take professional emails, for example. It used to be that I could just draft a quick message to the orchestra manager or the section leaders about, say, a bowing change in the violas or a shift in the rehearsal schedule, hit send, and be done with it. Now? Now I have to sit there and scrutinize every single word. I reread every decision I put in writing. I draft the email, I read it over, I get up and make a cup of coffee, and then I come back and read it again. Because I have to make absolutely sure there is zero ambiguity, no possible loophole they can use to come back later and say, "Oh, we misunderstood your instructions, Maestro, we thought you meant the *second* movement." I have to make my directives completely bulletproof. 

And rehearsals themselves... they are exhausting. I find myself constantly having to stop and ask for extra clarification from them. If the principal cellist asks a seemingly innocent question about a dynamic marking, I can't just give a quick answer and move on anymore. I have to ask them exactly why they are asking, what their interpretation was before they asked, and then I have to clarify my instructions three different ways just so they can't claim confusion later when they inevitably play it wrong. 

It’s like I’m doing two full-time jobs at once. I’m conducting the music, which, as I said, is already a monumental cognitive task, and I’m simultaneously playing this defensive game of administrative chess with the ensemble. Every email thread, every conversation about acoustics or scheduling... I have to double-check everything. So, yes, the main consequence is just how incredibly draining it is. It takes a massive toll on my energy reserves because I have to be so hyper-vigilant. But as far as actually functioning or losing my ability to manage my life? No, I’m still entirely capable. I haven't missed a single downbeat. I just have to work twice as hard to make sure they don't derail the performance.
Have you noticed yourself becoming emotionally flat or losing motivation for things you normally care about?

Emotionally flat? No. No, not at all. If anything, I think I’m... well, I’m probably more emotionally invested right now than I’ve ever been in my entire life. You can't be a music director—you can't compose or conduct—if you're emotionally flat. It just doesn't work. The whole point of the art form is to communicate feeling, right? 

When I'm looking at a score, especially this current commission, I am feeling every single tension and release in the harmony. I mean, just yesterday I was going over this incredibly delicate transition in the second movement, just this very exposed, fragile dialogue between the clarinet and the strings, and I was practically moved to tears just sitting alone at my desk because of how perfectly the voices weave together. I feel the music just as intensely as I always have. So, no, there's absolutely no flatness there. I'm incredibly dialed in to my emotions. 

And as for losing motivation... absolutely not. I haven't lost an ounce of motivation for the things I care about. Honestly, if anything, this whole situation with the ensemble has made me more determined. I care so deeply about this music, about getting it exactly right, that I refuse to let them ruin it. I wake up every single morning at 5:30 AM, I have my coffee, and I am immediately at my piano or reviewing the score, marking bowings, checking balances. I am fighting for this piece. 

If I didn't care, if I had lost my motivation, I would have just thrown my hands up months ago. I would have just let them play the tempos however they wanted, let them butcher the phrasing, and just collected my paycheck at the end of the season. It would be so much easier to just give up and let them have their way. But I can't do that. I won't do it. The music means too much to me, and my career means too much to me. So, no, I'm definitely not flat, and my motivation is... well, it's the only thing keeping me going, really. I have to see this through. I have to protect the work.
Outside of this ensemble, do you also find yourself suspecting that other people are trying to harm, exploit, or deceive you?

Other people? No, no, absolutely not. Not at all. I mean, my relationships with everyone else in my life are perfectly fine. Wonderful, actually. My family, my friends from conservatory, even just the people I interact with every day... I don't have any issues with them. I don't walk around thinking the whole world is out to get me, if that's what you're asking. 

Like, just last month, I guest-conducted a chamber group over in the next county for a weekend festival. It was an absolute dream. The players were responsive, the organizers were completely transparent about the scheduling, we had a fantastic time. If I were just... you know, a suspicious person by nature, wouldn't I have thought that festival board was trying to undermine me, too? But I didn't, because they weren't. We collaborated beautifully. And the barista at my local coffee shop—I don't think she's intentionally burning my espresso to ruin my morning. I know she's just making coffee. I trust my landlord, I trust my friends... 

And see, that's exactly why this situation with the ensemble is so incredibly frustrating to me. Because if I were just universally suspicious, or if the stress of the commission was just making me see shadows everywhere, it would bleed into the rest of my life, wouldn't it? I'd be looking over my shoulder at the grocery store. But it doesn't happen. It is strictly, exclusively, one hundred percent this specific group of musicians and their management. They are the only ones. So no, I don't suspect anyone else of trying to deceive me, because no one else is. It’s just them. And honestly, the fact that I can so clearly separate my normal, healthy relationships from what's happening in that concert hall is exactly how I know I'm right about what they're doing.
Have you become socially withdrawn since this began?

Socially withdrawn? No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, I make it a very specific point to maintain my social life. I mean, just this past weekend, I went out with a few guys from my conservatory days. We met up at this little Italian place downtown—the one right near the old practice halls, actually, we used to go there all the time after late-night theory seminars. We spent a good three, maybe four hours just catching up, talking about their current projects, arguing over Mahler interpretations, splitting a couple bottles of wine. It was completely normal, a really great time, actually. I certainly didn't feel any urge to hide away or cancel on them. 

I mean, yes, I am incredibly busy right now. And obviously, the situation with the ensemble takes up a massive amount of my mental bandwidth, as I've been explaining to you. So, sure, maybe I don't go out every single night like I might have when I was twenty-one and just starting my master's. But that's just the reality of being a working professional with a major commission on the table, not because I'm withdrawing from society or anything like that. 

If I were withdrawing, I'd be locking myself in my apartment, wouldn't I? Pulling the blinds down, ignoring my phone, letting my relationships wither. But my phone is always on. I'm always replying to texts from my friends. I still go to the gym every other morning and chat with the regulars, I still go to gallery openings when my friends in the visual arts have exhibitions... I haven't isolated myself in the slightest. I need those outlets, frankly. Being around normal, supportive people who aren't trying to sabotage my work is exactly what keeps me grounded right now. So, no, I haven't pulled back from my social life at all.
Have you felt that neutral things—like songs on the radio, TV programs, or strangers’ actions—were sending you special messages meant specifically for you?

Messages from the radio or TV? No. I mean, no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a movie, doesn't it? Like a spy thriller or something. No, when I turn on the radio, I hear music. I mean, usually I'm analyzing it—I can't help it, it's an occupational hazard. If a pop song comes on, I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, a I-V-vi-IV progression, how groundbreaking," or I'm listening to the production quality, the compression on the snare drum, the vocal tuning. But I'm certainly not sitting there thinking the singer is trying to tell me, I don't know, to buy a certain brand of cereal or that my life is in danger. It's just a song. It's just sound waves. 

And TV... I barely have time to watch TV anyway. When I do, it's usually just a documentary or maybe the news in the background while I'm cooking dinner. I'm not looking for hidden meanings in the anchor's tie color or the way the weather map is drawn. I know they're broadcasting to millions of people. It would be incredibly arrogant, really, to assume that out of all those viewers, the local news station is trying to beam a secret code directly into my living room. I mean, I'm a composer, not a secret agent. 

Even with strangers... look, if someone bumps into me on the sidewalk, I assume they were just looking at their phone and not paying attention, which, let's be honest, is what 90% of people are doing these days anyway. I don't think it's a coordinated effort to send me a message. People are wrapped up in their own lives. They're worrying about their rent, their kids, what they're going to have for lunch. They aren't spending their day trying to communicate with me through some elaborate pantomime. 

So, no, I don't experience anything like that. The only people who are actively trying to send me a message—and they're not exactly being subtle about it, honestly—are the musicians in that ensemble. And they aren't using the radio to do it; they're doing it right to my face in rehearsal by deliberately ignoring my tempo markings. That's a message, sure. "We don't respect you." But it's not a secret code. It's just blatant insubordination. But as for the rest of the world, no, I'm not looking for signs in the static. I'm just living my life, trying to write good music.
Before this started, were there any months when you became much less interested in work or in being around other people?

Less interested in work? Oh, no, absolutely not. I mean, if anything, it’s the exact opposite. You have to understand, in my field, in contemporary classical music, you can't really afford to just... lose interest. It's incredibly competitive. Ever since I finished my master's, I have been going non-stop. I mean, composing isn't just a job for me, it's—well, it sounds a bit cliché, I know, but it's a calling. I wake up thinking about orchestration, I go to sleep thinking about counterpoint. There hasn't been a single month, or even a week, really, where I just didn't care about it. 

If I had a month where I wasn't interested in working, I would have lost my commissions, I would have lost my grants. You have to constantly be hustling, writing, revising, meeting with artistic directors, pitching new concepts... it's a relentless pace, and I thrive on it. I always have. 

And as for being around people, no, not at all. Like I was saying earlier, I've always been very social. Networking is half the job, honestly. You have to go to the galas, you have to attend the premieres of your peers' works, you have to grab drinks with the principal cellist to make sure the bowings you wrote are actually playable. I've always loved that part of it. The collaboration, the energy of being in a room with other creatives... it's vital. 

Even before this whole mess with the ensemble started, I was always out and about. I mean, I remember last spring, I was juggling three different chamber pieces and still making time to host these big dinner parties at my place for my conservatory friends. I'd make this huge batch of mushroom risotto, we'd sit around debating the merits of atonalism versus neo-romanticism until two in the morning... It was fantastic. I've never been the brooding, isolated artist type. So, no, I've never had a period where I just withdrew or stopped caring about my work or my friends. I've always been completely dialed in. It's just... it's just this one specific group that's making things so difficult right now, not any lack of drive or interest on my part.
Have you had trouble keeping up with basic self-care, like showering or changing clothes?

Showering? Changing clothes? Oh, no, absolutely not. Not at all. I mean, I have a very strict morning routine, and I haven't deviated from it once. I get up, I make my pour-over coffee—usually a single-origin Ethiopian, I need that acidity to wake up my ears—and I immediately get in the shower. I couldn't imagine going to a rehearsal unwashed or wearing the same clothes as yesterday. Especially as a composer and a director, you have to present a certain image of authority, right? If I show up looking disheveled, they'd just use that against me, wouldn't they? They'd whisper, "Oh, look at him, he's falling apart, no wonder his score makes no sense." So, no, I am always impeccably dressed. I usually wear a nice dark turtleneck or a crisp button-down, very professional, very put-together. I haven't stopped taking care of myself in the slightest. 

But I will admit, the whole situation... it does take a toll in other ways. Not with my hygiene or my overall career—I haven't lost a single gig, I haven't missed a single deadline, let me be very clear about that. But the mental energy it requires? It's honestly exhausting. The main consequence of all this pushback I'm getting is that the actual rehearsals and my professional emails just take so much more energy than they used to. 

Take my emails, for instance. A few months ago, I could just shoot off a quick message to the ensemble manager or the section leaders: "Let's take measure 45 at 120 BPM, thanks." Done in ten seconds. Now? I sit there for twenty minutes drafting a three-sentence email. I have to reread every single decision I make, analyzing it from every possible angle to make sure I'm not giving them any loopholes to deliberately misinterpret my instructions. I find myself constantly having to ask for extra clarification from them, too, just to get it in writing that they understand exactly what I want. I'll have to say, "Did you receive the revised bowings for the cello section? Please confirm that you see the up-bow markings in measure 12." Just to make sure they can't claim ignorance later. 

And the rehearsals themselves... God, they just drain my energy completely. I have to be so hyper-vigilant on the podium. I can't just relax and let the music flow and trust the players like I used to; I'm constantly on edge, waiting for someone to intentionally drag the tempo or ignore a dynamic marking just to test me. So by the time I get home, my mental bandwidth is just totally fried. But like I said, I'm still showering, I'm still eating right, I'm still writing good music and getting paid for it. I just have to spend twice as much effort managing the logistics and the communications so they can't undermine the work.
Have you found it harder to start or carry through tasks, even when you want to do them?

Harder to start tasks? No, no, not really. I mean, like I was saying, outside of this whole exhausting issue with the ensemble, everything else is running exactly as it should. I still meet all my deadlines. I keep up with my composing perfectly fine. Actually, I just finished a rather complex piece a few days ahead of schedule, which took a massive amount of focus—lots of intricate counterpoint and layering—and I just sat down at the piano and got it done. So the drive to actually start the work and see it through is completely intact. You really can't survive in this industry if you can't self-motivate, you know? 

And it’s not just the music, either. I keep up with my personal life just fine. I still run most mornings. I have this loop I do around the neighborhood, usually about four or five miles, and I get out there and do it because physical discipline is important to me. It clears my head before I have to deal with the day's emails, gets the blood flowing. And things at home with my wife are basically steady, too. We have our routines, she has her own busy schedule, and we manage the household together without any issues. She hasn't had to pick up my slack or anything like that because I'm perfectly capable of doing what I need to do around the house. We still cook together, we still keep things organized. 

It really is just... it's just the mental toll of dealing with those specific musicians. When I have to sit down and draft those hyper-specific emails to the section leaders, sure, it feels like pulling teeth because I know they're going to scrutinize every single word to find a way to undermine me. It makes me dread opening my inbox, I won't lie to you. But I still do it. I don't just avoid the task or give up on it. I sit there, I write it, I double-check it from every angle, and I press send. So no, I don't have trouble starting things or carrying them through. I just resent how much unnecessary effort they're forcing me to put into the administrative side of things when I should just be focusing on the art. But my actual life? My writing, my running, my marriage? Everything else is completely on track.
Have you, over the past two years, become noticeably emotionally flat?

Emotionally flat? Oh, wow, no. Not in the slightest. I mean, if anything, I think I feel things almost too intensely sometimes. You really can't write a sweeping, three-movement chamber piece if you're emotionally flat, can you? It requires a massive amount of empathy and vulnerability. Just last week, I was working on this adagio section for a new string quartet, and I actually teared up a bit when I finally got the harmony to resolve exactly the way I was hearing it in my head. It was this beautiful, suspended dominant chord that just... well, anyway, the point is, I am deeply connected to my emotions. 

And it's not just the positive emotions, either. I mean, the sheer frustration, the—the anger, really—of dealing with this ensemble situation? I certainly don't feel numb or flat about that. When I see them deliberately ignoring my tempo markings, or when I get one of those passive-aggressive emails from the first violinist pretending she didn't understand a very basic bowing instruction, my blood absolutely boils. I get incredibly worked up, my heart races, because I care so much about the integrity of the performance. If I were emotionally flat, I'd probably just shrug and let them ruin the piece, right? But I can't do that. I fight for every single note.

If I show up looking disheveled, they'd just use that against me, wouldn't they? They'd whisper, "Oh, look at him, he's falling apart, no wonder his score makes no sense." Seen things? Like... hallucinations? No, absolutely not. I mean, my eyesight is perfectly fine, and I'm very grounded in reality. I have to be. So, no, no visions, no ghosts, no imaginary things floating around the room. I don't have any of that. I don't think I'd have the mental bandwidth to see things that weren't actually there, you know? I'm entirely too busy dealing with the things that are.
